The C melody saxophone is a woodwind instrument among the aerophones, Hornbostel–Sachs 422.212-71, pitched in C, a whole tone above the common tenor saxophone. Its body lies between the alto and the tenor, mostly with a curved neck although straight-necked versions exist; it sounds through a mouthpiece, and the bore gives it a more restrained timbre. Adolphe Sax designed it as part of his orchestral series, and in the early twentieth century it was found in amateur domestic playing, in hymn accompaniment in church, in Irish and Irish-American dance bands and in early jazz; it is rare today.

C調薩克斯風曾用於二十世紀初家庭、學校與城鎮樂團，也用於教堂聖詩伴奏。1920年: The C melody saxophone was used in homes, schools and town bands in the early twentieth century, and to accompany hymns in church. In the 1920s dance music and novelty numbers were often written for it, and it can be heard on early jazz recordings by Rudy Wiedoeft and Frankie Trumbauer; Jack Pettis used one in Ben Bernie's band. Irish and Irish-American dance bands used it often, since it made traditional tunes easy to play, and some guitar blues players chose it too. Big jazz bands did not make it a main part of their line-up.
C調薩克斯風源自阿道夫·薩克斯為管弦樂用途設計的C調與F調系列，20世紀初流行。: The C melody saxophone comes from the C and F series Adolphe Sax designed for orchestral use, and it was popular in the early twentieth century. It was made between 1914 and 1930 by firms such as Buescher and C. G. Conn, peaking around 1923; because it is non-transposing and its timbre is more veiled, it entered homes, schools, town bands, churches and Irish and Irish-American dance bands. Sales collapsed after the 1929 crash, and the big-band era preferred other saxophones, so production stopped around 1930. In the 1960s Leblanc made a small number under the Vito name, and in the early twenty-first century a small batch was revived in China for Aquilasax, ending in 2015.
C調薩克斯風音高較降B調次中音薩克斯風高一個全音，體積介於中音與次中音之間。其音: The C melody saxophone stands a whole tone above the B flat tenor and its size lies between the alto and the tenor. Its timbre is more restrained than that of the E flat alto or the B flat tenor, especially with its original mouthpiece, which suits playing at home. Loudness depends on the mouthpiece chosen; with a modern tenor or alto mouthpiece it may lose some of that restraint and become brighter with more acoustic energy, but the mouthpiece has to be tried with the instrument to keep the tuning.

初學者先裝配合適吹嘴，再持琴吹奏；彎頸款較常見，直頸款需將琴身稍離身體。吹嘴需試: A beginner first fits a suitable mouthpiece and then holds the instrument to play; the curved-neck version is the more common, and with a straight neck the body has to be held slightly away from the player. The mouthpiece must be tried with the instrument so that the tuning is not disturbed. Because it is a non-transposing instrument, ordinary sheet music can be read directly, but the range has to be watched. Practice can start in keys with easier fingerings, such as G and D major or E and A major.
